_comment: Country risk bands, cargo profiles and cover definitions used by the risk assessment stage. Edit this file to update the exercise — no code changes needed.
reviewNote: Bands reviewed against the public sources listed below. They are simplified teaching tiers, not an underwriting rating. Re-check before each course — a band that is right today can be wrong after a sanctions package or a conflict.
methodology: Each country sits in one of four bands. The band combines three things: the reliability of its logistics and customs (World Bank LPI), its maritime and inland security exposure (ICC-IMB piracy reporting and the Lloyd’s Joint War Committee listed areas), and whether it is under trade sanctions. A route score is the mean of the origin and destination bands, which is why a shipment from a band A country to a band D country scores the same as the reverse: the cargo is exposed to both ends.

sources.label: Logistics Performance Index
sources.informs: Customs, infrastructure and the reliability of transit times. Drives most movements between bands A, B and C.

sources.label: Piracy and Armed Robbery Against Ships
sources.informs: Maritime security exposure. The IMB counts actual and attempted attacks by location, which is why the exposure follows corridors rather than flags.

sources.label: Listed Areas — Hull, War, Strikes, Terrorism and Related Perils
sources.publisher: Lloyd’s Market Association, Joint War Committee
sources.informs: The reference underwriters actually use to decide where war risk is rated separately. Worth showing students: it is a list of waters, not of countries.

sources.label: EU Sanctions Map
sources.informs: Whether trade with a country is restricted. A sanctions listing places a country in band D on its own, whatever its infrastructure.

sources.label: Review of Maritime Transport
sources.informs: Trade volumes, fleet and the pressure on chokepoints such as Suez, Bab el-Mandeb, Malacca and Panama.

countryNotes.Russia: Band D on sanctions, not on infrastructure. Trade restrictions, payment channels and insurance availability are the binding constraints.
countryNotes.Ukraine: Band D. Active conflict; Black Sea routings and port availability change faster than any annual index can track.
countryNotes.Lebanon: Band D. Economic collapse and conflict exposure; Beirut port capacity remains reduced since 2020.
countryNotes.Libya: Band D. Fragmented governance and unreliable port operations.
countryNotes.Egypt: Band C. The country score is only part of the story: since late 2023 many carriers have routed around the Cape rather than transit the Red Sea, which lengthens transit and changes where the cargo is exposed.
countryNotes.Saudi Arabia: Moved from C to B in the September 2026 review. Sustained port investment and a clear LPI improvement. The Red Sea exposure is a corridor question, not a country one.
countryNotes.Oman: Moved from D to B in the September 2026 review. The old D reflected the Gulf of Aden, not Oman itself — Salalah and Sohar are well-run hubs. The corridor risk belongs to the water, not the flag.
countryNotes.India: Moved from C to B in the September 2026 review. India rose sharply in the 2023 LPI, helped by port turnaround times and the dedicated freight corridors.
countryNotes.Nigeria: Moved from D to C in the September 2026 review. The IMB has reported a sustained fall in Gulf of Guinea incidents since 2021. Inland security and port congestion keep it above band B.
countryNotes.Mauritania: Moved from D to C in the September 2026 review. Limited logistics capacity, but no armed conflict or sanctions driver to justify the top band.
countryNotes.France: Moved from B to A in the September 2026 review. Its LPI sits with Germany and the Netherlands; the old B was an inconsistency, not a judgement.

scoreLimits.title: What this score does not include
scoreLimits.body: This assessment uses six fields. It does not know your routing detail or whether the service tranships, your delivery deadline, the terms of your sales contract, your buyer’s quality protocol, the condition of the goods when they were loaded, or the season you are shipping in.
scoreLimits.closing: A risk assessment tells you what kind of shipment this is. It does not tell you what is wrong with yours.

C.label: Medium
C.note: Caution advised — check documentation and transit times.

D.label: High
D.note: Enhanced coverage needed. Political or security exposure.

general.label: General cargo
general.note: Standard goods with normal transport risk.

machinery.label: Machinery
machinery.note: Heavy equipment requiring special packing and lashing.

automotive.label: Automotive
automotive.note: Vehicle parts with specific handling requirements.

perishable.label: Perishable goods
perishable.note: Requires temperature control and fast transit.

electronics.label: Electronics
electronics.note: Sensitive to moisture, shock and pilferage.

hazardous.label: Hazardous materials
hazardous.note: Needs special handling, segregation and documentation.

recommendations.text: ICC (C) — minimal coverage is sufficient for this low-risk shipment.
ICC (B) — basic coverage recommended for moderate protection.
ICC (A) + carrier liability advised: the combination of route and cargo raises the exposure.
ICC (A) together with IWC and ISRCC extensions is strongly recommended for this high-risk scenario.

icca.reach: ICC (A) — all risks, subject to exclusions. Reaches theft, water damage and handling damage.
icca.name: ICC (A) — Comprehensive coverage
icca.text: Covers all risks of loss or damage to the cargo except the listed exclusions (war and strikes unless separately added, inherent vice, insufficient packing, wilful misconduct). The right choice for high-value or sensitive shipments.

iccb.reach: ICC (B) — major casualties plus water damage. Does not reach theft.
iccb.name: ICC (B) — Basic cargo coverage
iccb.text: Covers named perils: fire, explosion, stranding, sinking, collision, general average, jettison, water entering the vessel or container. Excludes theft, pilferage and most handling damage.

iccc.reach: ICC (C) — major casualties only. No theft, no water damage.
iccc.name: ICC (C) — Minimal cargo coverage
iccc.text: Covers major catastrophes only: fire, explosion, stranding, sinking, overturning, collision and general average sacrifice. Suitable for low-value, robust cargo on stable routes.

iwc.name: IWC — Institute War Clauses
iwc.text: Covers loss caused by war, civil war, hostilities, capture, seizure, derelict mines and torpedoes. Normally added on top of ICC (A) when the route crosses a listed high-risk area.

isrcc.name: ISRCC — Strikes, Riots and Civil Commotion
isrcc.text: Covers loss caused by strikers, locked-out workers, labour disturbances, riots, civil commotions and acts of terrorism. Recommended for volatile regions and for cargo dwelling in port.
